answers.question: lets brainstorm ideas for a po system for seikyo, 8 weeks of cover
answers.answer: The draft is a reasonable order and a poor system, and the reason is one row: Kameda Orange Big Pack had nothing on the shelf anywhere for all 90 days of the window, so its measured rate is what it sold while unavailable — the plan under-orders hardest exactly where the shelf failed hardest, and no rule you write can fix that from sales data alone. The window choice is the other half: the same eight weeks of cover asks for meaningfully different quantities depending on how far back demand is measured, which means the system's real design decision is a rule fixed once, not a judgement made per order. Two things it cannot settle, whatever you build: nothing records when goods actually arrive, so eight weeks of cover runs from the day you order rather than the day stock lands, and the supplier link is inferred from what has been bought from Seikyo before — most of what sells estate-wide traces to no supplier at all, so this is part of an order, never all of one. What I'd check next is Aji Assorted JP candy before it becomes the largest line: its stock records are negative, which is a broken count rather than a shortage, and what shows as on order comes from purchase orders still marked Open, which does not mean the goods have not arrived. Shall I fix the ninety-day window as the house rule and rebuild the draft against it?

answers.question: lets brainstorm ideas for a po system for seikyo, 8 weeks of cover
answers.answer:
**The demand window decides this order, not the cover.** One line — Aji Assorted JP candy, 729 units on the 90-day read — is most of the order on one window and absent on the other, so whatever you build has to make that choice explicitly rather than inherit a default. What none of this settles is when the goods land: nothing records when Seikyo deliveries arrive, so eight weeks of cover runs from today, not from the day stock hits the shelf — and 79 negative stock records sit behind these quantities, counted as nothing rather than as a debt. Products that sat empty sold less than they would have, and their rates are left as measured.

So the system needs four decisions it can't read off the data: the lookback, the treatment of stocked-out lines, whether unsold mapped products belong in the order, and a received date so cover means something. I'd hold at 90 days and hand-set the Aji Assorted line — shall I build that version out with values?

At 56 days of cover Seikyo comes to 48 sellable lines, and **the draft is one line plus a long tail**: Aji Assorted JP candy alone wants 729 units against 14.7 a day, where the next largest line is 191. Two things to settle before this becomes a system: a chunk of the stock records behind it are negative — broken counts, not shortages — and 18 of these products spent time with nothing on any shelf, so their measured rates are what they sold while available, not what they'd have sold; also, nothing in the data records when Seikyo's goods actually arrive, so eight weeks of cover currently starts the day you order, not the day it lands.

Say whether the eight weeks should run from delivery rather than from today, and I will rebuild the draft with the lead time you name.

items.message: 92 stock records behind these figures are negative, which is a broken record rather than a shortage. Stock has been counted as none at those locations rather than as a debt, so the quantities here are not inflated by them. The raw figure is on each row as on_hand_raw.

18 of these products had nothing on the shelf anywhere for at least one day in the window — the worst, Aji Assorted JP candy, for 90 days. Their sales rate is what they sold while available, so it understates what they would have sold. answers.answer: Here's a working draft at 8 weeks of cover: 48 Seikyo products that sold in the last 90 days, and **28 of them are already at zero cover** — nothing on any shelf today, so the order is catching up rather than covering forward. The one decision that matters is Aji Assorted JP candy: 731 units suggested on its own, against roughly 15 a day. Two design points for the system itself — nothing records when Seikyo goods actually arrive, so any cover you pick starts from today, not landing day; and 31 of these products were out somewhere in the window, so their measured rate is what they sold while available, which understates the reorder for exactly the items you most want to fix.The draft is on the board. items.message: Nothing records who supplies a product. This plan is built from what has been bought from Seikyo SEK001 before, and across the whole business 450 of the 787 products that sold in the last 90 days cannot be traced to any supplier at all. This is part of an order, not all of one.
items.guidance: The link is purchase_order_lines -> purchase_orders.supplier_name. A declared supplier per product would close the gap.

items.message: 149 stock records behind these figures are negative, which is a broken record rather than a shortage. Stock has been counted as none at those locations rather than as a debt, so the quantities here are not inflated by them. The raw figure is on each row as on_hand_raw.

31 of these products had nothing on the shelf anywhere for at least one day in the window — the worst, Kameda Orange Big Pack, for 90 days. Their sales rate is what they sold while available, so it understates what they would have sold. The rate has not been adjusted: raising a measured figure to what it might have been would be inventing a sale.

What is shown as on order comes from purchase orders still marked Open, and Open does not mean not received — some carry notes saying the goods arrived. Some of that quantity may already be on the shelf.
Nothing records when goods actually arrive, so none of this allows for the wait between ordering and delivery. Whatever cover you choose starts from today, not from the day the stock lands.
